claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an as-reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and nano- to microscale phase heterogeneity.
High-resolution electron microscopy and chemical mapping can provide quantitative descriptors such as grain size, phase-boundary statistics, phase distributions, and local chemical fluctuations.

A deep-neural-network surrogate using imaging-derived descriptors, thermophysical constraints, and a limited set of tensile and fracture tests can accurately predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness in HfNbTiVAl10.
Imaging-derived microstructural descriptors can serve as model inputs alongside physically validated mechanical tests and thermophysical calculations.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase geometry mediate local stress distributions and crack-initiation sites.
Microstructure-sensitive features control elastic response, plastic flow, and eventual crack initiation.
Encoding microstructure-sensitive features in a surrogate permits it to bypass computationally intensive atomistic or thermodynamic integrations.
Physics-informed constraints from thermophysical calculations and fracture mechanics enable rapid interpolation and extrapolation across compositional and microstructural space.
The proposed model will reduce relative errors in Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by 30–50% compared with CALPHAD or pure first-principles benchmarks.
The proposed model will reduce computational time by at least a factor of ten relative to baseline methods.
Under validated conditions, predicted tensile and fracture trends will closely match experimental data.
First-principles calculations can be combined with experimental elastic and plastic deformation measurements in refractory high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD, full thermophysical calculations, and high-fidelity first-principles methods are computationally expensive.
First-principles and ordered-compound machine-learning approaches have limited fidelity for predicting fracture toughness.
The model remains reliable only when key microstructural descriptors stay within approximately ±10% of the training domain.
Large changes in phase fractions, interface coherency, or nanoscale chemical fluctuations can make the model unreliable.
Emergent brittle secondary phases outside the training regime can make the model unreliable.
The projected 30–50% accuracy gain and tenfold efficiency gain are based on analogous physics-informed machine-learning applications in related high-entropy alloys.
Fracture-toughness prediction is particularly difficult because toughness is sensitive to microstructural flaws.

The hypothesis is falsified if any held-out prediction exceeds 10% error for modulus, 15% for yield strength, or 20% for fracture toughness, or if computational time is not reduced by at least tenfold.
